intro: The weather station on the summit has been automated for forty years, and its forecasters now spend their shifts tending the archive rather than the sky. This morning its printer woke up and produced something that is definitely not a forecast, but a column of typewritten lines of wildly uneven length. The senior forecaster, who files the station's annual reports in a drawer of pigeonholes cut to take one folder each, stood the pages upright in a spare row of holes and found, with the mild triumph of a man who has spent a career matching things to their places, that every page stood straight and none was left over.
echo: Poe sent a fisherman down a whirlpool off the coast of Norway.

puzzles.title: Beaufort Twelve
puzzles.flavor: Only the count of each run was kept.
hints: The numbers describe runs of filled squares. What picture could they be drawing?
Paint by numbers. The picture is written, not drawn.

puzzles.title: Inversion
puzzles.flavor: Room numbers in a hotel where nobody reads with their eyes.
hints: Write each number in binary. Six yes-or-no choices: is there an alphabet built from exactly that?
Braille: each bit is one of the six dots (1, 2, 4 down the left column; 8, 16, 32 down the right).

puzzles.title: Rain Shadow
puzzles.flavor: It never travels in a straight line, and neither does the truth.

blocks.text: The knight sets out from h4: Ng6 Ne5 Nd7 Nf6 Ng8 Ne7 Nd5 Nb6 Nc8.

hints: Those are chess moves. Which squares does the piece land on, and what's written there?
Start on the given square, play each move, and read the letter on every square it lands on.

puzzles.title: Wind Chill
puzzles.flavor: Shredded, then sorted by a very tidy intern.
hints: The strips are alphabetised, not in order. The word lengths say where the breaks fall. Which strip could start the sentence?
Chain the strips into one string and split it by the word lengths; the sentence tells you what to submit.

puzzles.title: Shipping Forecast
puzzles.flavor: Everyone has a place. Everyone pays for it in their own name.

clues: Aubrey and Hamish sit side by side.
Hamish sits somewhere between Aubrey and Ursula.
Hamish sits somewhere between Charles and Gertrude.
Ursula sits somewhere to the left of Gertrude.
Exactly one person sits between Francis and Ursula.

hints: Only one arrangement satisfies every clue; start from whoever has an end seat or a fixed neighbour. Once they're seated, why might the seat numbers matter?
Solve the seating, then take the k-th letter of the name in seat k, left to right.

puzzles.title: Anvil Cloud
puzzles.flavor: Take stock of everything you recognise.

blocks.text: Hidden in the grid: 8 words to do with the weather station.

hints: Once every theme word is found, is anything left unclaimed? Read it in order.
Find the theme words; the letters no word uses, read row by row, are the answer.
The hidden words are: BALLOON, BREEZE, CIRRUS, FRONT, FROST, HAIL, ISOBAR, SQUALL.

puzzles.title: Squall Line
puzzles.flavor: Turn the wheel until it talks.

blocks.text: ALEX XLI GSYVMIV GEVVMIH AEW RSX KSPH SV WIGVIXW FYX E WMRKPI ASVH VEHEV

hints: Try moving every letter the same distance. How far turns the short words into English?
A Caesar shift: find the one shift that fixes a short word, then apply it everywhere.

puzzles.title: Dew Point
puzzles.flavor: Heard over the radio from the other side of the glass.
hints: Each word stands for a letter, the way radio operators spell. Do those letters read? If not, try the alphabet backwards.
Take the NATO call signs' initials, then swap each letter for its mirror: A for Z, B for Y.

puzzles.title: Red Sky At Night
puzzles.flavor: Shaken, one word at a time.
hints: Each word is complete but shuffled. Start with the shortest ones: does a sentence appear?
Unscramble each word where it stands; the sentence tells you what to submit.

meta.title: Meta: Isobars
meta.flavor: Everything at the weather station has a place.
hints: The grid's rows are all different lengths. So are your answers.
Put each answer in the row its length fits; read the shaded squares top to bottom.
